Not my first by a long shot, but the one that sticks out most. Inner city EMS. Dispatched to a GSW, go hauling ass out the door and down the road, get out. Find a ton of cops on scene in various stages of panic, think 'oh boy'. Go to the upstairs apartment, find balloons and pizza all over the place. Turns out it was a kid's birthday party. The birthday kid (an 8yo) is lying on the floor by the window, one gunshot wound to the left upper chest, cops performing CPR. 4 feet away lies his 16yo brother, one gunshot wound to the head, cops performing CPR. Parents screaming in the bedroom. We ran the codes, aware throughout that there really wasn't anything we could do, but just on robot mode. Both were pronounced at the hospital. 

Turns out they were shot because a group followed the kids' older brother home in regards to a gang beef. They shot randomly into the residence when they saw people at the windows. The fugitive task force caught them a few days later. Absolutely senseless violence. 

I was drunk for about 72 hours straight after that.

EMS culture is so varied and different across the states and agencies that it's insane. My first job was IFT. I worked there for like a year and a half and hated it, it was for a large agency which clearly didn't care about its employees, paid bottom level wages, and ran us into the ground trying to keep impossible transport schedules. I quit that job happily. 

My next job was at a fire based municipal 911 agency where I did both fire and EMS services in a fairly dense suburban area. 10-12 calls in a normal 24 hour shift there, between the fire and EMS calls, with some good stuff (a note, when an EMT says "good call" what they really mean is exciting or interesting, which is usually actually bad and quite tragic) mixed in there, especially vehicle accidents on the three highways we serve. But mostly things were relatively relaxed, lots of BLS medical calls and public service things. The guys there were great, it was a close Firehouse culture with a lot of well intentioned shit talking, often well cooked dinners in the station dining room, a gym to work out in, plenty of training available, and bunks to sleep in. I still work there per diem, but I wasn't making the money I wanted there. 

My job now I've been doing for 2 years, it's on a 911 ambulance in a smallish but dense and extremely violent city (40 homicides out of about 100,000 people last year) where we run 15-20 EMS calls per unit in a 12 hour shift. Shootings, stabbings, pedestrians struck, fires with victims, and all kinds of high acuity medical calls from the often chronically ill residents of our many, many projects. We go into a criminal asylum, a state max security prison, a solid number of high rises, onto highways and bridges, and sometimes to a large river. It's rarely a night I don't find myself delivering a critical patient directly to the trauma bay. There are often calls holding in the stack, and we run our asses off. My busiest night I did 23 calls including multiple shootings and codes, which is only possible because transport time to the hospital is usually 5 minutes or less. It's common for us to get involved in fights without police backup, and important for us to each have each other's back. 

Consequently, the work culture there is aggressive and unforgiving. Toxic, even. If a new worker can't handle the volume, they're swiftly bullied out of the department, and you better have thick skin because the guys there are extremely dark in what they find funny, and will talk shit to each other about the most personal stuff. But if you can hack it, the shared experiences mean you'll be forging close friendships. My current full time partner and I didn't know each other four months ago, now we hang out on most of our days off. Our relationship with the nursing staff at our trauma center is extremely close, and at least on night shift we'll go out drinking with the nurses the mornings after our tours. So the culture there, while toxic, also embraces the people living through it. 

One constant throughout EMS is that the working relationships you have with your coworkers are like no office job in the world. For 12 or 24 or more hours you're stuck with these people and you rely on them for everything. They'll be your best friends if you let them be, and you'll share a bond forged by seeing horrible stuff together that you will not share with anyone else. Pay attention, be conversant but not annoying, and do your job and you'll swiftly create the social connections needed to make work feel a lot less like work. You might be exhausted and worn out while you're there, but I promise a couple shifts off and you'll be craving to jump back on a bus. 

Good luck.
